title: Science · Non-exam content (Terms 1–3)
exam_focus: Revision of the Term 1–3 modules not in the Year 10 yearly exam: Earth's energy, genetics, motion, reactive chemistry, nuclear reactions, climate science and organic chemistry.

questions.stem: Which two types of solar radiation reach the surface of the Earth and act as the main driving force for Earth's processes?
questions.explanation_en: The main drivers of Earth's processes that reach the surface are visible light and infrared radiation: visible light provides energy for photosynthesis, and infrared radiation heats the hydrosphere, driving the water cycle. X-rays and microwaves are mostly absorbed by the atmosphere and do not reach the surface.
questions.source: Term 1 · Earth's Energy – Earth.pdf（Topic 6 Earth · Solar radiation）

questions.stem: Which of Earth's four spheres is described as the outer part of the Earth, consisting of the crust and upper mantle and about 100 km thick?
questions.explanation_en: The lithosphere = crust + upper mantle, approximately 100 km thick. The atmosphere is a layer of gas, the biosphere is the range of biological survival, and the hydrosphere is the solid/liquid/gaseous water on the surface.
questions.source: Term 1 · Earth's Energy – Revision Booklet（Topic 6 Earth · Terminology）

questions.stem: Arctic sea ice melts and exposes the dark ocean underneath. Which statement best explains the effect on global temperature?
options: Albedo increases, so more radiation is reflected and the temperature falls.
Albedo decreases, so more solar radiation is absorbed and the temperature rises further.
Albedo stays the same because water and ice reflect the same amount of radiation.
Albedo decreases, so more radiation is reflected back to space and the temperature falls.
questions.explanation_en: Albedo ranges from 0 to 1, with whiter surfaces being more reflective. As ice melts, exposing dark seawater, the albedo decreases, absorbing more solar radiation, and the temperature rises, accelerating ice melting and forming a positive feedback loop.
questions.source: Term 1 · Earth's Energy – STUDENT 5. Earth.docx（Practical 2 Albedo Effect）

questions.stem: Explain how solar radiation drives the water cycle.
questions.answer: Infrared radiation from the Sun warms the hydrosphere, so liquid water evaporates into water vapour. The vapour rises and cools, condenses into clouds, and eventually falls back to the surface as precipitation such as rain, hail or snow.
questions.explanation_en: The energy for the water cycle comes from solar infrared radiation heating the hydrosphere: evaporation → rising, cooling, and condensation → precipitation, returning water to the oceans, lakes, and rivers.
questions.source: Term 1 · Earth's Energy – Earth.pdf（Topic 6 · The Water Cycle）

criteria.t: States that infrared radiation from the Sun warms the hydrosphere, so liquid water evaporates into water vapour
States that the vapour rises and cools and condenses into clouds
States that the water returns to the surface as precipitation such as rain, hail or snow

questions.stem: Which statement best defines a gene?
options: A whole chromosome containing many genes
A section of DNA that codes for a protein
An inherited disease passed on to offspring
A compound that stores energy in all cells
questions.explanation_en: A gene is a segment of DNA that encodes a protein. A chromosome is a form of DNA organisation (23 pairs in humans), and DNA is composed of nucleotides; the three are not at the same level.
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – Revision Booklet（Topic 8 Genetics · Terminology）

questions.stem: A section of DNA has the base sequence AGT TAC CTG. What is the sequence of the complementary DNA strand?
questions.explanation_en: DNA complementary base pairing is A-T and G-C, so AGT becomes TCA, TAC becomes ATG, and CTG becomes GAC, and options containing U are mRNA sequences, not complementary DNA strands.
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – 2020 Year 10 Yearly Examination Answers（Part D Q3）

questions.stem: In a sample of DNA, 30% of the bases are adenine. What percentage of the bases is guanine?
questions.explanation_en: Given A=T, T also makes up 30%, totaling 60% for both, and the remaining 40% is split evenly between G and C, so G makes up 20%.
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – 2020 Year 10 Yearly Examination Answers (Part D Q4) + base-pairing rules

questions.stem: Distinguish between mitosis and meiosis in terms of the number of daughter cells produced and the chromosome number in each daughter cell.
questions.answer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells and is used for growth and repair of body cells. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.
questions.explanation_en: Mitosis produces 2 diploid daughter cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces 4 haploid gametes for sexual reproduction (23+23=46 to restore diploidy).
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – Genetics.pdf（Knowledge 2 · Compare mitosis and meiosis）

criteria.t: States that mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells
States that meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell
Relates the difference to purpose: mitosis for growth and repair of body cells, meiosis for sexual reproduction

questions.stem: One extra base is inserted into the middle of a gene. Which statement best describes the likely effect on the protein produced?
options: Only the codon containing the extra base is affected; the rest of the protein is normal.
The reading frame shifts, so every codon after that point may code for a different amino acid.
There is no effect because the genetic code is degenerate.
The DNA double helix can no longer be replicated.
questions.explanation_en: Codons are read in groups of three bases, and inserting one base will shift all subsequent codons (frameshift), usually greatly altering the protein sequence, and only inserting a multiple of 3 bases will affect just one amino acid.
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – Genetics.pdf（Knowledge 3 · Frameshift - Insertion）

questions.stem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed, and tall (T) is dominant over short (t). What fraction of the tall offspring is expected to be heterozygous?
questions.explanation_en: For Tt x Tt, the ratio is 1TT:2Tt:1tt, or 3:1 for tall to short plants, and since the question asks for the ratio within the tall plants (3 parts), the heterozygous Tt makes up 2/3 of them.
questions.source: Term 1 · Genetics – Half Yearly Revision.pdf (Punnett squares: genotype and phenotype ratios)

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 300 m in 20 s. What is the cyclist's average speed?
questions.explanation_en: The speed is v = d/t = 300m / 20s = 15 m/s, and 0.067 m/s is the result of inverting the formula (20/300), while 320 m/s is the sum of the two numbers.
questions.source: Term 1 · Motion – Speed and Velocity Problem Solving Jan 10（v = d/t）

questions.stem: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation_en: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, and is a vector; distance, speed, and time only have magnitude, and are scalars, as are velocity and force.
questions.source: Term 1 · Motion – Half Yearly Revision.pdf（Scalar vs Vector）

questions.stem: A motorcycle travelling at 25 m/s accelerates at 7.0 m/s² for 6.0 s. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation_en: The final velocity is v_f = v_i + at = 25 + 7.0 * 6.0 = 25 + 42 = 67 m/s, and 42 m/s is just the change in velocity, forgetting to add the initial velocity, while 175 m/s is 25 * 7, using the wrong operation.
questions.source: Term 1 · Motion – Acceleration Problems (Practice) (Question 10)

questions.stem: On a velocity–time graph, what does the gradient (slope) of the line represent?
questions.explanation_en: The slope of a v-t graph is Δv/Δt = acceleration, and the area under the line represents displacement, which is a common point of confusion (area vs slope).
questions.source: Term 1 · Motion – SG 1.1 Study Guide（velocity–time graph）

questions.stem: A 1200 kg car travelling at 20 m/s brakes and comes to rest in 5.0 s. Calculate (a) its acceleration and (b) the net force acting on it.
questions.answer: a = (v_f − v_i)/t = (0 − 20)/5.0 = −4.0 m/s², so the car decelerates at 4.0 m/s². F = ma = 1200 × (−4.0) = −4800 N, that is, a net force of 4800 N opposite to the car's motion.
questions.explanation_en: First use the acceleration formula (final velocity minus initial velocity divided by time, with a negative sign for deceleration), then substitute into F = ma, with a net force of 4800 N in the opposite direction of motion.
questions.source: Term 1 · Motion – Half Yearly Revision.pdf (DESA: average acceleration and F = ma)

criteria.t: Calculates the acceleration as a = (0 - 20)/5.0 = -4.0 m/s2, i.e. the car decelerates at 4.0 m/s2
Calculates the net force with F = ma, giving 4800 N acting opposite to the car's motion

questions.stem: Magnesium is added to hydrochloric acid and a gas is produced that gives a 'pop' when a lit splint is held to it. Which gas is this?
questions.explanation_en: Acid + metal produces salt + hydrogen gas, which can be tested with a lit wooden splint (pop test), whereas acid + carbonate produces CO2, which requires a lime water test.
questions.source: Term 2 · Reactive Chemistry – Term 3 Reactive Chemistry Week 5 Answers（Acid-Metal Reaction）

questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to hydrochloric acid. Name the type of reaction and write the word equation.
questions.answer: This is a neutralisation reaction. The word equation is: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water.
questions.explanation_en: Acid + base produces salt + water, a neutralization reaction, where the metal part of the salt comes from the base (Na⁺) and the nonmetal part comes from the acid (Cl⁻), resulting in sodium chloride.
questions.source: Term 2 · Reactive Chemistry – Term 3 Reactive Chemistry Week 7 Answers（Neutralisation Reaction）

criteria.t: Names the reaction as a neutralisation reaction
Writes the word equation: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water

questions.stem: Using collision theory, why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: Particles gain kinetic energy, so more collisions succeed.
The particles get larger, so they collide more often.
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered.
The concentration of the reacting particles increases.
questions.explanation_en: The collision theory requires particles to collide with sufficient force and in the correct direction.
questions.source: Term 2 · Reactive Chemistry – 2020 Year 10 Yearly Examination Answers (Part A Q7 — collision theory)

questions.stem: Copper carbonate is added to nitric acid. Write the word equation, name the salt formed, and describe how you would test for the gas produced.
questions.answer: copper carbonate + nitric acid → copper nitrate + water + carbon dioxide. The salt formed is copper nitrate. Bubble the gas through limewater; if the limewater turns milky (chalky white), the gas is carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation_en: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide; the second part of the salt's name comes from the acid (nitric acid → nitrate), so it's copper nitrate.
questions.source: Term 2 · Reactive Chemistry – Term 3 Reactive Chemistry Week 7 Answers（balanced equations / acid-carbonate）

criteria.t: Writes the word equation: copper carbonate + nitric acid -> copper nitrate + water + carbon dioxide
Names the salt formed as copper nitrate
Describes testing the gas by bubbling it through limewater, which turns milky if the gas is carbon dioxide

questions.stem: Which set of coefficients correctly balances this equation: __Al + __HCl → __AlCl₃ + __H₂ ?
questions.explanation_en: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂: the number of atoms on the left side is Al 2, H 6, Cl 6, and on the right side is Al 2, Cl 6, H 6, making them equal.
questions.source: Term 2 · Reactive Chemistry – Term 3 Reactive Chemistry Week 7 Answers（Balanced Equations part 2）

questions.stem: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both atoms of carbon. How do the two atoms differ?
options: The number of electrons in a neutral atom
questions.explanation_en: Isotopes refer to atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
questions.source: Term 2 · Nuclear Reactions – atomic_models_interactive_v2.html（Isotopes）

questions.stem: In the core of a main sequence star such as the Sun, hydrogen nuclei are combined to form helium, releasing large amounts of energy. What is this process called?
options: Chemical combustion of hydrogen in oxygen
questions.explanation_en: The sun's core is about 15 million °C, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei, releasing enormous energy, which is the source of the sun's radiation.
questions.source: Term 2 · Nuclear Reactions – The Universe 2020.pptx (Main Sequence Star) + Revision Booklet Topic 6 (definition of solar radiation)

questions.stem: Explain how scientists use radioactive carbon (carbon-14) in the remains of a once-living organism to work out when it died.
questions.answer: While an organism is alive it continuously takes in small amounts of radioactive carbon dioxide from the air. When it dies the intake stops, so the radioactive carbon slowly decays into the non-radioactive form. Measuring how much radioactive carbon is left in the remains therefore shows how long ago the organism died.
questions.explanation_en: Living things constantly take in radioactive carbon; after death, the intake stops, and the remaining radioactive carbon decays at a fixed rate, allowing us to calculate the time of death.
questions.source: Term 2 · Nuclear Reactions – Year 10 - Evolution.pptx（Techniques used to date fossils · Absolute dating）

criteria.t: Explains that a living organism continuously takes in small amounts of radioactive carbon from the air
Explains that the intake stops at death, so the radioactive carbon slowly decays into the non-radioactive form at a fixed rate
Explains that measuring how much radioactive carbon is left in the remains shows how long ago the organism died

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the enhanced greenhouse effect from the natural greenhouse effect?
options: The natural greenhouse effect is caused by human activity, while the enhanced effect is caused by volcanic eruptions.
The enhanced greenhouse effect only occurs when the ozone layer is destroyed.
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming caused by human activities releasing abnormally high amounts of greenhouse gases.
The natural greenhouse effect stops all infrared radiation from leaving the atmosphere.
questions.explanation_en: The natural greenhouse effect is the absorption of infrared radiation by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, keeping the Earth's temperature relatively stable.
questions.source: Term 3 · Climate Science – Term 3 Earth Week 1 Answers（natural vs enhanced greenhouse effect）

questions.stem: Which gas is a colourless, odourless, incombustible greenhouse gas formed during respiration, combustion and the breakdown of dead organic material?
questions.explanation_en: The answer is carbon dioxide, as methane is combustible and nitrogen and argon are not the main greenhouse gases or products.
questions.source: Term 3 · Climate Science – 2020 Year 10 Yearly Examination Answers（Part B Q2）

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an adaptation strategy rather than a mitigation strategy?
options: Building wind farms to generate electricity without coal
Installing solar panels on the roofs of houses
Painting roofs white to mimic the albedo effect
Capturing and storing carbon dioxide from power stations
questions.explanation_en: Mitigation involves reducing emissions and stabilising atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, while adaptation involves reducing social vulnerability to the impacts that are already happening.
questions.source: Term 3 · Climate Science – Revision Booklet（Topic 6 · Mitigation / Adaptation strategies）

questions.stem: Extra carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater and forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions. Why does this harm shellfish?
options: The hydrogen ions compete with the shells for carbonate ions, so shellfish cannot build their shells.
The hydrogen ions dissolve the calcium carbonate shells by raising the pH of the water.
The extra carbon dioxide warms the water so the shellfish cannot respire.
The carbonic acid removes calcium from the water so shellfish absorb more carbonate.
questions.explanation_en: An excess of H⁺ ions will combine with carbonate ions to form bicarbonate, competing with shell formation for carbonate ions, making it harder for shells to form.
questions.source: Term 3 · Climate Science – Term 3 Earth Week 2 Answers（Ocean Acidification）

questions.stem: Large areas of Arctic permafrost are thawing. Explain why this is described as a positive feedback that makes global warming worse.
questions.answer: Frozen soils store large amounts of organic carbon and methane. When the permafrost thaws, microbes break this material down and release carbon dioxide and methane, which are both greenhouse gases. These extra gases trap more heat, which thaws even more permafrost, so the warming reinforces itself.
questions.explanation_en: The chain reaction is: permafrost thawing → microbial decomposition → release of CO₂ and methane → enhanced greenhouse effect → warming → more permafrost thawing, creating a positive feedback loop.
questions.source: Term 3 · Climate Science – SCNSW10CH00393.pdf (Global systems · permafrost) + Revision Booklet (permafrost methane)

criteria.t: Explains that frozen permafrost soils store large amounts of organic carbon and methane
Explains that when the permafrost thaws, microbes break this material down and release carbon dioxide and methane, which are greenhouse gases
Explains the loop: the extra gases trap more heat, which thaws even more permafrost, so the warming reinforces itself

questions.stem: Which name is correct for a straight-chain alkane containing six carbon atoms?
questions.explanation_en: The prefix hex- indicates 6 carbon atoms, and the suffix -ane indicates an alkane, so it's hexane.
questions.source: Term 3 · Organic Chemistry – KATZ - WEEK 3 LESSONS（Lesson 3 Naming Organic Compounds）

questions.stem: Which of the following is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.explanation_en: The general formula for alkanes is CnH2n+2 (e.g. C5H12 when n=5), while alkenes are CnH2n and alkynes are CnH2n−2, with the last being alcohol classes (containing the -OH functional group).
questions.source: Term 3 · Organic Chemistry – Year 10 Organic Chemistry Homework Worksheet（Part C Q6）

questions.stem: Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions, and why the smaller molecules are collected near the top of the column.
questions.answer: Crude oil is heated so that most of it vaporises, and the vapours rise up the fractionating column, which is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction condenses at the level where the temperature falls below its boiling point. Smaller molecules have lower boiling points, so they rise further and are collected near the top.
questions.explanation_en: Distillation uses the difference in boiling points: the temperature inside the tower decreases from bottom to top, and each component condenses at a height where the temperature is lower than its boiling point, with smaller molecules having lower boiling points and rising higher to the top (LPG, gasoline), and larger molecules remaining at the bottom (asphalt).
questions.source: Term 3 · Organic Chemistry – KATZ - WEEK 3 LESSONS（Lesson 2 Fractional Distillation）

criteria.t: Explains that crude oil is heated so most of it vaporises and the vapours rise up the column, which is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top
Explains that each fraction condenses at the level where the temperature falls below its boiling point
Explains that smaller molecules have lower boiling points, so they rise further up the column
Concludes that the smaller molecules are therefore collected near the top of the column

questions.stem: What is the correct IUPAC name of the compound CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃?
questions.explanation_en: The longest carbon chain has 4 carbon atoms (butane), with a methyl branch attached to the 2nd carbon; numbering must start from the end closest to the branch to get the smallest possible position number, so it's 2-methylbutane, and 3-methylbutane is an incorrect name for the same molecule numbered from the other end.
questions.source: Term 3 · Organic Chemistry – Year 10 Organic Chemistry Homework Worksheet（Part G Q12）

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C₅H₁₀. Could it be an alkane?
options: No, because alkanes follow CnH2n+2, which for five carbons is C₅H₁₂ and not C₅H₁₀.
Yes, because it contains only carbon and hydrogen.
Yes, because any compound with five carbon atoms always has ten hydrogen atoms.
No, because it does not contain enough hydrogen to be a hydrocarbon at all.
questions.explanation_en: Substituting n=5 into the alkane formula CnH2n+2 gives C5H12; C5H10 has two fewer hydrogens, matching CnH2n, which is an alkene (or cycloalkane), and can't be a straight-chain alkane.
questions.source: Term 3 · Organic Chemistry – Year 10 Organic Chemistry Homework Worksheet（Part N Q32）
